More information about the BRIUMVI Patient Support program can be accessed at www.briumvipatientsupport.com. ABOUT MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS Relapsing multiple sclerosis (RMS) is a chronic demyelinating disease of the central nervous system (CNS) and includes people with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) and people with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (SPMS) who continue to experience relapses. RRMS is the most common form of multiple sclerosis (MS) and is characterized by episodes of new or worsening signs or symptoms (relapses) followed by periods of recovery. It is estimated that nearly 1 million people are living with MS in the United States and approximately 85% are initially diagnosed with RRMS.1,2 The majority of people who are diagnosed with RRMS will eventually transition to SPMS, in which they experience steadily worsening disability over time. Worldwide, more than 2.3 million people have a diagnosis of MS.1 ABOUT TG THERAPEUTICS TG Therapeutics is a fully integrated, commercial stage, biotechnology company focused on the acquisition, development and commercialization of novel treatments for B-cell diseases. In addition to a research pipeline, TG Therapeutics has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for BRIUMVI® (ublituximab-xiiy) to treat adult patients with relapsing forms of multiple sclerosis (RMS), including clinically isolated syndrome, relapsing-remitting disease, and active secondary progressive disease, as well as approval from several regulatory agencies outside of the U.S. for BRIUMVI to treat adult patients with RMS who have active disease defined by clinical or imaging features. title: What Is Sales Enablement Content? A Guide for Content Marketing Teams
summary: Sales enablement content gives buyers and sales teams useful answers at key decision points. Learn what to create, how to build it, and how to measure whether
body_text: What Is Sales Enablement Content? A Guide for Content Marketing Teams Sales enablement content is material that helps a sales team have better, more relevant buyer conversations — a category guide, a case study, an implementation overview, a competitive comparison, or a simple answer to an objection that keeps appearing on calls. It sits between public marketing and private conversation, carrying enough substance that a reader can verify a claim without needing a meeting to translate it. For content teams, the job isn't to turn every blog into a sales asset. It's to understand where a buyer needs more context or a different form of explanation, then build the material that serves that moment. Start with the buying questions that keep returning The easiest way to fill an enablement library with useless material is to start with formats. "We need a battlecard." "We need a case-study template." None of those describes the decision the buyer is actually trying to make. Start with questions instead. What does a buyer misunderstand before a first call? Which objection appears after the demo? What implementation concern slows an evaluation? What does an internal champion need to explain to a CFO or technical stakeholder? Group the questions by stage and stakes. Some need a broad public guide because people search for them before they know the company exists. Some need a clear product page because the buyer is testing fit. Some belong in a private sales document because they only make sense inside a late-stage evaluation. We make a version of this argument in our content marketing guide : different queries warrant different content, and the same principle holds after a lead enters the funnel. The question determines the asset, not the other way around. The core sales enablement content types Most B2B teams need a compact set of recurring asset types: a category or problem guide for shared language, a product or use-case page for how the work happens, a comparison page for tradeoffs, an implementation guide to reduce risk, a case study to give a claim a human setting, and a concise internal one-pager a champion can carry into another room. Each asset should do one primary job. A page trying to define the market, compare every option, prove the ROI, and close the deal will usually bury the useful part. Link the category guide to the practical guide. Link the practical guide to proof. Link proof to a conversion page or sales conversation. Google's link guidance pushes for descriptive anchors for a reason — "read how lead routing works for multi-segment B2B teams" tells a reader more than "learn more." Sales enablement works the same way. Build from actual company knowledge Sales enablement becomes generic when the content team has no access to the people doing the work. A product marketer might understand the broad positioning but miss the detail that makes an implementation guide trustworthy. A sales leader might know the objection but not have time to turn it into a resource. Create a repeatable capture system: call notes, product demos, customer-success retrospectives, support patterns, and interviews with technical experts. Ask for concrete examples, where the workflow gets difficult, and what buyers often assume incorrectly. Then edit the material for a real reader. Raw expert knowledge isn't automatically useful content — it's often too dense or too cautious to answer the question outright. We built our content review workflow around this loop: comments from one review inform future drafts and related pages, so the learning improves the whole system rather than closing out with a single approval thread. Give sales context when someone converts The enablement asset and the lead handoff should be connected. When a reader fills out a form after visiting a category guide, a case study, and a product page, that behavior is useful context, not a complete statement of intent. Sales should know what the person was reading and whether the form answers point to a particular segment or use case. Our guide to lead capture and routing for B2B SaaS covers why the handoff should weigh more than a single lead source — product interest, account status, and behavior all shape the right response, provided the team treats content engagement as context rather than a mind-reading device. A rep doesn't need to say "I saw you read three blog posts." They can offer the next useful resource and skip re-explaining the category from scratch. Measure use, movement, and gaps Enablement content needs a record of use: which assets sales shares, which pages buyers revisit, which assets appear around meetings and opportunities, and where reps still ask for something new that doesn't exist yet. Avoid overclaiming attribution. A buyer may read a guide, attend a demo, talk to peers, and convert months later — no dashboard recovers every influence perfectly, though it can still show patterns. Our guide to attribution and incrementality recommends separating observed, inferred, modeled, and unresolved results, and that same discipline applies here: a rep sharing an asset is observed, a revenue number assigned solely to the document deserves far more caution. Keep the library alive enough to trust Enablement content decays fast when it touches pricing, integrations, or competitor context. Assign owners, add last-reviewed dates, and give sales a way to flag anything inaccurate or missing. The library also needs to be findable. If getting the right asset means asking three people for a Drive link, reps will stop using it consistently, and a public site where guides, proof, and product detail link together clearly matters just as much as internal organization. Sales enablement content works when a buyer has fewer avoidable questions and a rep has a better way to answer the ones that remain. Build it around real decisions, give each asset one clear job, and keep it connected to the content and lead systems around it — a folder of collateral can't do that work by itself.

title: Background Verification for Logistics and Warehousing in India: How to Stop Shrinkage Before It Starts
summary: Reduce warehouse shrinkage with fast background verification for logistics workers using PAN, Voter ID, and licence checks.
body_text: Insights & Resources Background Verification for Logistics and Warehousing in India: How to Stop Shrinkage Before It Starts August 5, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet Somewhere in a fulfillment centre outside Bhiwandi right now, a contract worker is scanning packages, loading pallets, and moving inventory worth crores through a facility the size of multiple football fields. This worker was hired 48 hours ago during a peak season surge. The labour contractor said he was reliable. His Aadhaar photocopy is in a file somewhere. Nobody verified it against a database. Nobody checked if the name on the document actually belongs to the person wearing the warehouse vest. This scene plays out thousands of times every day across India’s booming logistics sector. The industry employs over 22 million people and is growing at over 14 percent annually, fueled by e-commerce, quick commerce, and third party logistics. India’s e-commerce logistics market alone was valued at over $19 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $103 billion by 2034. But this explosive growth has exposed a critical vulnerability that costs the industry crores every year: inventory shrinkage caused by unverified workers. Shrinkage, the gap between inventory records and actual stock, eats 2 to 5 percent of logistics margins. A significant portion of this shrinkage is internal, caused by pilferage and theft by workers who were never properly identified or verified. Organized cargo theft rings have been documented placing unvetted contract workers into fulfillment hubs during peak hiring spikes, specifically to exploit the chaos of high volume operations. This guide is for logistics company owners, warehouse managers, supply chain heads, and HR teams in the logistics sector. We will cover why background verification is the most effective tool against shrinkage, what checks you need for different warehouse roles, and how to verify workers at the speed your operations demand. Why Logistics and Warehousing Has a Unique Verification Problem The logistics industry faces verification challenges that most other sectors do not encounter. Extreme Hiring Velocity During major peak periods like Diwali sales, Republic Day promotions, or end of season clearances, a single fulfillment centre may need to onboard 500 to 2,000 contract workers in less than 72 hours. Traditional background verification that takes a week per candidate is physically impossible at this speed. This creates an impossible choice for warehouse managers: either slow down operations and miss delivery targets, or bring in unverified workers and accept the risk. Most choose the latter. And that is exactly when shrinkage spikes. High Turnover and Transient Workforce Warehouse worker turnover in India can exceed 100 percent annually. Workers move between facilities, switch from one logistics provider to another, and alternate between warehouse work and other informal employment. Many work at multiple facilities simultaneously during peak seasons. This transient workforce makes traditional verification approaches impractical. By the time a comprehensive background check returns results, the worker may have already moved on to another facility. Multiple Layers of Contractors Most large logistics operations do not directly employ their warehouse workers. They use staffing agencies and labour contractors who recruit, deploy, and manage the workforce. This creates the same accountability gap seen in construction: the logistics company assumes the contractor verified the workers, the contractor assumes the sub contractor did it, and nobody actually verifies anyone. High Value, Portable Inventory Warehouses are filled with products that are small, valuable, and easy to steal. Electronics, cosmetics, clothing, mobile accessories, and pharmaceutical products can be worth significant amounts per unit and are easy to conceal. Unlike raw materials in a factory, these are finished consumer goods with immediate resale value. A warehouse worker processing 500 packages per shift has hundreds of opportunities to divert a product. Without proper identity verification, the worker is essentially anonymous, making theft a low risk proposition. Round the Clock Operations Modern fulfillment centres operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Night shifts typically have fewer supervisors and less management oversight than day shifts. This reduced supervision during night operations creates additional opportunities for unverified workers to exploit. The True Cost of Shrinkage in Indian Logistics Let us quantify the problem. If a warehouse processes Rs 50 crore worth of inventory annually and experiences 3 percent shrinkage, that is Rs 1.5 crore in losses every year from a single facility. A logistics company with ten warehouses could be losing Rs 15 crore annually to shrinkage across its network. Not all shrinkage is caused by theft. Damaged goods, receiving errors, and administrative mistakes also contribute. But internal theft by workers is consistently identified as one of the top causes, and it is the one most directly addressed by background verification. Beyond direct inventory losses, shrinkage creates several cascading costs. Insurance premiums increase as claims rise. Customer satisfaction drops when orders go missing. Brand reputation suffers when a logistics partner cannot guarantee delivery. Investigation costs accumulate as incident after incident requires security team involvement. And the cost of installing additional surveillance, security checkpoints, and loss prevention measures adds up quickly. What Background Checks Logistics Companies Should Run The verification approach for logistics and warehousing needs to balance thoroughness with speed. Here is a practical framework designed for the realities of the industry. For All Warehouse Workers (Including Contract and Temporary Staff) Every person who enters a warehouse floor should have their identity verified. No exceptions for peak season hires, no shortcuts for “the contractor’s people,” no skipping verification because the person is “only here for two weeks.” PAN Card Verification. Verify the PAN number against the Income Tax Department database. Confirms the worker’s name and date of birth. This is the fastest way to confirm that the person’s identity document is genuine. Voter ID Verification. Validate the EPIC number against the Election Commission database. Provides identity and registered address confirmation. Many warehouse workers hold Voter IDs even if they do not have PAN cards. ID Verify by SalaryBox (verify.salarybox.in) runs both checks against government databases and returns results in minutes. The pay per check pricing means you can verify every worker affordably, even during peak season surges when you are onboarding hundreds of workers in a single day. For Drivers and Transport Staff Anyone who operates vehicles, drives delivery trucks, or handles goods in transit needs additional verification. Driving Licence Verification. Confirms licence validity, vehicle class authorization (critical for heavy goods vehicles), and any suspensions or endorsements. A driver operating a 16 wheel truck with an expired or fake licence is a liability and safety crisis waiting to happen. For Supervisors and Team Leads Workers in supervisory roles have greater authority and often control inventory access points. Add deeper checks. UAN Verification. Check against EPFO records to verify employment history. This reveals previous employers and employment dates, confirming whether the supervisor actually has the experience they claim. A supervisor who fabricated their work history may lack the judgment and skills needed to manage a warehouse team. Cross Record Analysis. Compare details across multiple identity documents. ID Verify by SalaryBox does this automatically, flagging discrepancies in names, dates of birth, or other details across PAN, Voter ID, and Driving Licence records. For Warehouse Managers and Operations Heads Senior roles with full facility access and financial authority warrant comprehensive verification. Criminal Record Check. Search court records for any history of theft, fraud, or financial crimes. A warehouse manager with an undisclosed criminal background involving property crimes is an unacceptable risk. Address Verification. Confirm current residential address through database checks or physical verification. How to Verify Workers at Warehouse Speed The logistics industry cannot afford week long verification timelines. Here are practical strategies for verification at the speed your operations demand. Gate Level Digital Verification Set up a verification station at the warehouse entry point. When a new worker arrives, they provide their PAN or Voter ID number. The site administrator enters the details into ID Verify by SalaryBox and gets results in minutes. If the check passes, the worker receives a warehouse access badge. If there is a discrepancy, the worker is held back until the issue is resolved. This process adds approximately five minutes per worker. For a batch of 50 new workers, the entire verification can be completed in a single morning. Pre Deployment Verification by Contractors Make digital identity verification a contractual requirement for all staffing agencies and labour contractors. Include a clause in your contractor agreements specifying that all workers must be verified through government database checks before deployment to your facility. Provide your contractors with access to the verification platform. When a contractor recruits a new worker, they verify the identity before adding the person to their deployment roster. By the time the worker arrives at your warehouse, they are already verified. Batch Processing During Peak Season During major sale events, you might onboard hundreds of workers in a single day. Use batch processing to handle the volume. Collect identity document numbers from all arriving workers, run verification in bulk, and sort workers into verified and pending categories. Deploy verified workers immediately and process pending cases as a priority. Biometric Integration For warehouses with biometric access control, link the verification record to the biometric profile. This ensures that the person whose identity was verified is the same person who enters the facility each day. It also prevents a common trick where a verified worker shares their access credentials with an unverified friend. Addressing the Contractor Accountability Gap The multi layered contractor structure in logistics creates one of the biggest verification gaps. Here is how to close it. Contractual Requirements Add specific verification clauses to every contractor and staffing agency agreement. The clause should specify that all workers deployed to your facility must have PAN or Voter ID verified against government databases before deployment, the contractor must maintain verification records and make them available for audit, workers who cannot be verified must not be deployed, and the contractor is liable for any losses caused by workers they deployed without proper verification. Random Audits Periodically audit your contractors’ verification records. Pull a random sample of deployed workers and check whether their verification records exist and are genuine. This keeps contractors honest and demonstrates that you are serious about enforcement. Direct Verification Layer Even with contractor verification requirements, run your own identity checks at the gate level. This double verification creates a safety net. If the contractor’s process had gaps, your gate level check catches them. Industry Specific Scenarios E-Commerce Fulfillment Centres E-commerce fulfillment centres process high volumes of consumer electronics, fashion, and personal care products. Workers handle individual items during picking, packing, and sorting. The opportunity for pilferage is highest during packing, when workers are handling open packages. Verify every worker’s identity, and implement zone based access controls so workers can only enter the areas they are assigned to. Cold Storage and Pharmaceutical Warehousing Cold storage facilities and pharmaceutical warehouses handle temperature sensitive and high value inventory. A single shipment of vaccines or specialty medicines can be worth crores. Workers in these facilities need enhanced verification including criminal record checks, because the potential financial impact of theft is enormous. Third Party Logistics (3PL) Providers 3PL companies manage inventory on behalf of their clients. When a client’s product goes missing from a 3PL warehouse, the 3PL company bears the financial and reputational liability. This makes verification not just a risk management tool but a competitive differentiator. 3PL companies that can demonstrate robust worker verification win more contracts and retain clients longer. Quick Commerce and Dark Stores Quick commerce operations (Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart) use small dark stores with minimal staff. Each worker in a dark store handles a larger proportion of the inventory compared to a mega warehouse. A single unverified worker in a dark store with 5 to 10 employees has significant access and minimal oversight. Verify every person. Last Mile Delivery Hubs Last mile hubs are the final staging point before packages reach customers. Workers at these hubs sort and dispatch thousands of packages daily. Missing packages at the last mile stage are a major source of customer complaints and financial loss. Identity verification for every worker at these hubs is essential. Building a Shrinkage Prevention Strategy That Works Background verification is not the only tool against shrinkage, but it is the foundation. Here is how it fits into a comprehensive shrinkage prevention strategy. Layer 1: Verify identity. Every worker’s identity is confirmed through government database checks before they access the facility. This is the baseline. Layer 2: Control access. Zone based access controls limit each worker to the areas they need for their role. Verified identity linked to biometric access ensures the right person enters the right zone. Layer 3: Monitor inventory. Real time inventory tracking, CCTV coverage, and exception reporting catch discrepancies as they happen rather than during monthly audits. Layer 4: Investigate and act. When discrepancies are detected, verified identity records make investigation faster and more effective. You know exactly who was in each zone at each time, and you have confirmed identity information for every person. Without Layer 1 (verification), the other layers are significantly less effective. Camera footage of an unverified worker is almost useless because you do not know who you are looking at. Access logs for workers with fake IDs tell you nothing. Verification is what makes every other security measure actionable. Frequently Asked Questions How quickly can logistics workers be verified? Digital identity verification through ID Verify by SalaryBox takes minutes per worker. PAN and Voter ID checks run against government databases and return results almost instantly. Even during peak season surges, a single administrator can verify 50 to 100 workers in a few hours using digital verification. Is it practical to verify contract and temporary workers? Yes, and it is essential. Contract and temporary workers handle the same inventory as permanent employees. They pose the same theft risk. The fact that they are temporary actually increases the risk because they have less loyalty to the employer and less to lose if caught. Digital verification is fast and affordable enough to make it practical for every temporary hire. What is the ROI of background verification in logistics? If verification prevents even a fraction of your shrinkage losses, the ROI is enormous. Verifying 1,000 workers through PAN and Voter ID checks costs a fraction of a single high value theft incident. Companies that implement systematic worker verification consistently report reductions in shrinkage rates. Should we verify workers who are only here for a few days? Yes. Some of the most significant theft incidents involve workers who are deployed for short periods specifically to steal. A worker who is “only here for three days” during a sale event has access to the same inventory as someone who has been there for three years. Three days is more than enough time to cause significant losses. How do we handle verification for workers who arrive at 2 AM for a night shift? Set up your verification process to work 24/7. Digital verification through ID Verify by SalaryBox works any time. The night shift supervisor or security team can run verification checks at the gate regardless of the hour. What if a contractor refuses to verify their workers? A contractor who refuses to verify workers is a contractor who is cutting corners. This is a red flag for the quality and reliability of their workforce. Consider switching to a contractor who takes verification seriously, or implement your own gate level verification as a non negotiable requirement. Stop the Leak Before It Drains Your Margins Every unverified worker in your warehouse is an unknown risk walking past your inventory. Every shift without proper verification is another opportunity for shrinkage. The logistics industry runs on thin margins, and shrinkage from unverified workers eats directly into your profitability. ID Verify by SalaryBox (verify.salarybox.in) gives you verification at warehouse speed. Run PAN, Voter ID, and Driving Licence checks in minutes. Verify one worker or a thousand. Pay only for what you use. No subscriptions, no minimum orders, no sales calls. Protect your inventory. Verify your workforce. title: Flexport Ocean Timeliness Indicator
summary: Discover Flexport APIs and EDIs to speed, scale, and optimize your supply chain. Developer tools make it easy to instantly access logistics data and vital cargo and global trade documentation in the Flexport Platform or your ERP.
body_text: Week to July 20 2026: Transit time from China to the US West-Coast decreased by 1.0 days, falling from 37.1 to 36.1 days. The China to North Europe route saw a 1.0-day decrease, moving from 56.9 to 55.9 days. Lastly, the transit time to North Europe decreased by 0.8 days, falling from 74.5 to 73.7 days. Transit times from China to the US West-Coast and China to North Europe both experienced modest decreases. Please direct questions about the Flexport OTI to press@flexport.com . The Methodology: The Flexport Ocean Timeliness Indicator (OTI) utilizes data from Flexport’s ocean shipping operations for an expansive view of the cargo’s journey. Updated on a weekly basis, the Flexport OTI shows the transit time from the cargo ready date at the exporters’ factory or warehouse to the containers’ departure from the destination ocean port. The ocean shipping world tends to run along “trade lanes.” The three biggest east-west trade lanes carry goods from Asia to the U.S. West Coast, Asia to the U.S. East Coast, and from Asia to Northern Europe. The OTI captures the timeliness of each. As there are many transit time nuances from port to port and service to service, to show accurate trends, the OTI uses the following logic: Excludes premium services. Displayed transit times are based on a trailing two-week median. Major origin and destination ports are used as a proxy for the overall trade lane to create clear trends. Other origin or destination ports will have additional transit time considerations based on ocean carrier services . Asia to U.S. West Coast trade lane uses the China ports of Shanghai and Ningbo and the U.S. West Coast ports of Los Angeles/Long Beach. Asia to U.S. East Coast trade lane uses the China ports of Shanghai and Ningbo and the U.S. East Coast ports of New York/New Jersey and Norfolk. Asia to North Europe trade lane uses the China ports of Shanghai and Ningbo and the North Europe port of Rotterdam.
